wv_endless_wall.blurb: Endless Wall is a long, nearly unbroken sandstone cliffline in the New River Gorge, close to Fayetteville, West Virginia. The rock is hard Nuttall sandstone, and the wall stretches for roughly three miles at heights from about sixty to over a hundred feet, so the climbing feels exposed and has big views. Sport and trad are close to evenly split, with a little bouldering at a couple of spots. Grades begin near 5.7 and reach 5.14, but most routes fall between 5.10 and 5.12, and easy bolted lines are scarce. The wall is divided into lettered sections, with The Cirque, Party Buttress, Fern Point and Honeymooner's Area among the busiest. Spring and fall are the most comfortable seasons, although The Cirque can be good in January and one section works in August.

_expect.name: Laramie Peak Wildlife Habitat Management Area

wy_laramie_peak_wildlife_habitat_managem.blurb: This part of the Laramie Range lies in eastern Albany County, Wyoming, at around 7,000 feet, and it is a quiet, little-known corner of the range. Reese Mountain is the heart of it, built of granite with long crack and face lines, and it holds about half of the climbing. The surrounding gneiss is often mistaken for granite. Sport routes outnumber trad by roughly two to one, with a few aid lines mixed in. Grades run from low fifth class up to 5.13, though the bulk sits between 5.10 and 5.11, with a fair number of 5.8 and 5.9 lines too. Other clusters include Kennedy Ranch Rocks, which offers roadside sport climbing on granite, plus Douthitt Mountain, Toaster Wall and Sugar Loaf.

ab_moose_mountain.blurb: Moose Mountain is a limestone sport climbing area in Kananaskis Country, Alberta, a short drive from Calgary, with its crags strung along Canyon Creek Road in forest. Nearly everything here is bolted. Grades cluster firmly in the 5.10 and 5.11 range, with a smaller group of 5.12s and 5.13s and a thin spread of easier lines from 5.7 upward. Rock quality is uneven and can change within a single route, so choose lines with care. Most crags face south, which lets them warm up on cool days and keeps them climbable into spring and fall, while a few developed cliffs sit on the shadier side of the canyon. Painted Wall Far Right, Moose Patch, Morning Side and Larry's Gym are among the larger sectors.

ca_lake_arrowhead_area.blurb: Lake Arrowhead Area gathers crags around the mountain town of Lake Arrowhead, in the San Bernardino Mountains of Southern California, at roughly 5,200 feet. The mountains here are mostly granite, mostly good quality though some of it is grainy in the manner of Joshua Tree, and climbing is chiefly single-pitch. Sport and trad are both well represented, with a small amount of top-rope. Grades run from low fifth class up to 5.12, centered on 5.9 through 5.11, so moderate and intermediate climbers have plenty to do. Lake Arrowhead Pinnacles hold most of the climbs, with Sphinx Rock, Scot Rock and Seely Creek making up the rest. Newer routes can be a little dirty or lichen-covered.

wy_wind_river_range.blurb: The Wind River Range runs northwest to southeast for roughly 100 miles along the Continental Divide in western Wyoming, a remote, largely roadless range of glacier-carved lakes and cirques. It is built on granite, and the high exposed faces are the draw, with Cirque of the Towers, Titcomb Basin and the Deep Lake area among the best-known zones. Most routes are long alpine rock climbs, backed by some trad, bouldering, and a little ice and mixed climbing. Difficulty spans class 3 and 4 scrambles through to 5.13, though most rock climbing sits between 5.8 and 5.11. Mountain weather can turn severe in any month, and steep fourth and fifth class ground, rockfall and bears all deserve respect.

pa_haycock_mountain_nockamixon.blurb: Haycock Mountain rises above Lake Nockamixon in northern Bucks County, Pennsylvania, near Quakertown, and its slopes are strewn with diabase boulders that formed from an intrusion of magma about 200 million years ago. It is purely a bouldering destination, with hundreds of problems. Grades start at V0 and reach into double digits, with the deepest supply from V0 through V5 and a steady tail of harder lines above that. The problems are scattered across the hillside in many zones, including Caves Trail, Hangar 18, Gateway and Teddy Bear Area. Rain or snow makes the rock slippery and fragile, so dry days are the ones to aim for, and a crash pad and a partner are standard.
